reason: Start by building the canal sensors for head rotation.
expectation: The turning sensors will fit into the fluid-filled canals, forming a structure that detects head rotation.

alternatives.reason: The weighted membranes could form the other balance organ, but either branch seems a reasonable start.

effect: The canals and sensors form rotation-sensing organs; I can build the other balance organ before connecting their pathways.
reaction: The link between changing a turn and fluid bending the sensors is clear, though the picture description is brief.
reason: Build the complementary sensors for tilt and acceleration.
expectation: The weighted membranes will sit over the hair cells and help them respond to tilt and acceleration.

alternatives.reason: I could connect the rotation organs to the nerve pathway first, but I want to build both sensor types.

effect: The weighted gel bends hair bundles during tilt or changes in straight-line motion, completing the second sensor type.
reaction: The before-and-after comparison makes the distinction from steady motion clear.
reason: Combine the two balance organs before connecting their signals.
expectation: I expect a combined balance-organ structure containing both rotation and gravity-and-acceleration sensors.

alternatives.reason: I could connect the rotation sensors to nerves first, but combining the two organs seems more direct.

effect: The rotation and gravity-and-acceleration sensors are now grouped as balance organs beside the cochlea.
reaction: The combined location is clear, though the result adds little explanation.
reason: Connect the balance organs to the nerve pathways carrying their signals toward the brainstem.
expectation: The combined organs will gain vestibular nerve connections; reflex pathways may still need connecting.

alternatives.reason: Connecting the nerve pathways to reflex circuits first also seems possible, but I prefer to start at the sensors.

effect: Both sensor types now send signals through vestibular nerves to brainstem circuits; the reflex connections remain to be added.
reaction: The distinct pathways converging on brainstem circuits make the integration clearer.
reason: Connect the sensory pathways to the reflex circuits for eye movement and posture.
expectation: The balance signals will connect to brainstem pathways controlling eye movements and postural muscles; the assembly may still need to be added to the body.

alternatives.reason: I could attach the organs to the body first, but completing the reflex connections seems more direct.

effect: The balance organs now connect through the brainstem to eye-movement and postural circuits; they still need to be added to the body.
reaction: The branching pathways clarify the two reflex destinations, though their movements are not yet shown.
reason: Attach the completed balance pathways to the body; this is the only available combination.
expectation: The body will gain connected balance organs and reflex pathways, completing the goal.

effect: The completed body shows how balance signals contribute to stabilizing the eyes and adjusting posture, alongside other sensory information.
reaction: The opposite eye movement makes the reflex's practical purpose clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the reflex pathways to the body was most worthwhile: the paired head views give the constructed pathways a clear functional outcome.

leastWorthwhile.text: Grouping the two balance organs added little explanation beyond placing them beside the cochlea.

surprise.text: The weighted-gel comparison clarified that the otolith organs respond to changes in straight-line motion, not simply steady movement.

arbitrary.text: No action seemed purposeless, though grouping the organs before connecting them felt mostly like an assembly step.

continue.text: I would continue: the progression from sensor mechanics to a visible reflex made me curious about how other sensory systems guide movement.
